html:
After his awakening, the Buddha spent about 45 years teaching across the Ganges plain, in the 5th century BCE by most modern estimates. His dates are uncertain, and many scholars now place his death near 400 BCE.

His first sermon, at the deer park of Sarnath near Varanasi, set out the Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; and the way to end it is the Eightfold Path of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Around this he taught that all things are impermanent and that there is no fixed, lasting self.

He taught in everyday languages, not in the priests' Sanskrit, and rejected the idea that animal sacrifice or birth as a Brahmin made anyone holy. That set him alongside other wandering teachers of the age who broke with the Vedic order: Mahavira of the Jains, and the Ajivikas.

He built an order, the sangha, of monks and later nuns, who lived on alms and followed a code of rules. Kings and merchants gave it land and halls. King Bimbisara of Magadha was a patron, and a rich merchant bought a park at Shravasti where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons.

After his death his monks met at Rajagriha, in the First Buddhist Council, to recite his sayings and rules together so they would be remembered. That spoken body of teaching was handed down for centuries before it was written.
sum: After his awakening, the Buddha spent about 45 years teaching across the Ganges plain, in the 5th century BCE by most modern estimates. His dates are uncertain, and many scholars now place his death near 400 BCE.
